passages.t: Cornelius, a centurion who feared God
passages.happening:
At Caesarea there is a man named Cornelius, “a centurion in what was called the Italian Regiment” (verse 1). He and his whole household are devout and God-fearing. He gives generously to the poor and prays to God regularly (verse 2).

One afternoon, at about the ninth hour, he sees an angel of God in a clear vision. The angel says, “Cornelius!” He stares in fear and asks, “What is it, Lord?” (verses 3-4). The angel answers, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God” (verse 4). He tells Cornelius to send men to Joppa for a man named Simon, called Peter, who is staying with Simon the tanner by the sea (verses 5-6).

Cornelius calls two servants and a devout soldier, tells them everything, and sends them to Joppa (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
Caesarea was a port city on the coast, built by Herod the Great and named after the emperor Caesar Augustus. Most of its people were not Jewish. It was where the Roman governors of Judea lived, so Roman soldiers were stationed there.

A centurion was an officer in the Roman army, in charge of a unit of about a hundred men (often fewer in practice). Luke says Cornelius belonged to the ‘Italian Regiment’. An inscription names an Italian cohort (a unit of several hundred soldiers) serving in Syria around AD 69, some years after this. Whether the same unit was at Caesarea at this time is not known, and scholars differ.

To a Jewish hearer, a Roman officer was a sign of the power that ruled over them. Yet Luke describes this one with the warmest words he has. He is ‘devout and God-fearing’, he gives to the poor, and he prays. In Luke's Gospel another centurion was praised by Jewish elders because ‘he loves our nation and has built our synagogue’ (Luke 7:5).

‘God-fearing’ is the key word. Luke uses it for Gentiles (people who were not Jewish) who worshipped the God of Israel. They prayed to him, gave to the poor, and often attended the synagogue, but they had not been circumcised or become Jews. Such people are named again in Acts 13. Later inscriptions point the same way: one from the city of Aphrodisias, in what is now Turkey, probably from the third century, lists donors to the Jewish community and names some as ‘God-fearers’ after the Jews. Scholars debate how far that inscription matches Luke's use of the word.

The ninth hour was about three in the afternoon, the time of the afternoon sacrifice at the temple and a regular hour of Jewish prayer. Cornelius prays when Israel prays.
passages.ot:
The angel says that Cornelius's prayers and gifts have gone up ‘as a memorial offering before God’. That is the language of the temple. In the Law a ‘memorial portion’ of a grain offering was burned on the altar, rising to God (Leviticus 2:2). Cornelius cannot offer at the altar in Jerusalem, but God counts his prayers and his gifts to the poor as an offering.

The prophets had said that God's house would be open to such people: “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7). And Scripture had long said that God sees what others overlook: “man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.asks: Cornelius did what he knew to do: he prayed, and he gave to people in need. God met him there and led him further. Ask whether you are faithful with the light you already have. And notice that God did not ask Cornelius to find the truth alone. He sent him to someone who could tell him.

passages.happening:
The next day, at about noon, as the men are nearing Joppa, Peter goes up on the roof to pray (verse 9). He becomes hungry, and while the meal is being prepared, he falls into a trance (verse 10).

He sees heaven open and something like a large sheet being let down by its four corners. In it are all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles and birds (verses 11-12). A voice says, “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” (verse 13).

“No, Lord!” Peter answers. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean” (verse 14).

The voice speaks a second time: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (verse 15). This happens three times, and then the sheet is taken back up into heaven (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Houses in that land had flat roofs, used as extra living space. A roof was a quiet place to pray. The sixth hour was about midday.

The sheet holds animals of every kind, clean and unclean mixed together. The Law of Moses divided animals into ‘clean’ ones that Israel could eat and ‘unclean’ ones that it must not eat (Leviticus 11). Pigs, for example, were unclean. These food laws were one of the clearest marks of being Jewish. Jews kept them at great cost, and many still keep them today with love and care, as a way of honouring God in daily life.

So Peter's answer is not stubbornness. It is faithfulness. He has kept these laws all his life, as his parents did and as God commanded. ‘Impure’ here translates a Greek word meaning ‘common’, the opposite of holy. To be told to kill and eat would have felt like being told to betray his God.

Three times the voice speaks. Peter would remember another ‘three times’: the night he denied Jesus three times, and the morning by the lake when Jesus asked him three times, ‘Do you love Me?’ (John 21:17).
passages.ot:
The food laws were given to set Israel apart. God said, “You are therefore to distinguish between clean and unclean animals and birds”, and, “I have set you apart from the nations to be My own” (Leviticus 20:25-26). The line between clean and unclean food was a picture of the line between Israel and the nations.

Faithful Jews had held that line under pressure. Daniel, in a foreign king's palace, “made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine” (Daniel 1:8). The prophet Ezekiel said, as Peter does here, “No unclean meat has ever entered my mouth” (Ezekiel 4:14). Peter's ‘No, Lord’ stands in that line of faithfulness.

That is why the vision shocks. It touches the very picture God had given of Israel's calling to be set apart.
passages.hard:
What does the vision mean for the food laws? Christians read it mainly as being about people, with the food question following from it.

Peter himself gives the meaning a few verses later: “God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean” (verse 28). The vision prepares him to enter the house of a Gentile and eat at his table. When he retells it in chapter 11 and again at the council in chapter 15, his point is that God ‘made no distinction between us and them’ (15:9).

The food question follows. Mark, writing his Gospel, comments on Jesus' teaching that what goes into the stomach does not make a person unclean: “(Thus all foods are clean.)” (Mark 7:19). Paul writes, “All food is clean” (Romans 14:20). So most Christians do not keep the food laws of Leviticus, and believe they are not required to. Some Christians, including many Jewish believers in Jesus, keep them gladly as part of their Jewish life, as the thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem were ‘zealous for the law’ (21:20). Paul asked both kinds of believers to welcome one another and not to judge each other over food (Romans 14).

None of this treats the food laws as foolish. God gave them, and they did their work: they kept Israel set apart for centuries, so that the promised Messiah would come from a people who knew the one God. Jewish families who keep them today are honouring the God of Abraham. The vision is not a story about Jews being wrong. It is a story about God widening his table.
passages.asks: Peter was faithful, and God still had something new to show him. Ask whether there is a line in your own life that you have drawn around ‘people like us’, and whether God might be asking you to step over it. Being right about God's past commands does not mean you have understood all of his purposes.

passages.happening:
While Peter is still puzzling over the vision, the men from Cornelius find Simon's house and call out at the gate, asking for Simon called Peter (verses 17-18).

The Spirit says to Peter, “Behold, three men are looking for you” (verse 19). He tells Peter to go down and go with them “without hesitation, because I have sent them” (verse 20).

Peter goes down. “Here am I, the one you are looking for,” he says. “Why have you come?” (verse 21). They tell him that Cornelius, “a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation” (verse 22), has been told by an angel to hear a message from him.

So Peter invites them in as his guests. The next day he sets out with them, with some of the believers from Joppa (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The timing is exact. While Peter is still wondering what the vision means, the answer knocks at the gate. God has prepared both men, each without the other knowing.

The messengers are careful to say that Cornelius has ‘a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation’. They know that a Jew might be wary of a Roman officer's call, so they speak of his respect for Jewish people.

Then Peter does something small that is not small at all: he invites them in as his guests. To give a meal and a bed to Gentiles, two of them servants and one a soldier, is the first step of what the vision meant. Peter is learning by doing.

He also takes some believers from Joppa with him. Later we learn there were six (11:12). They will be witnesses of what happens.
passages.ot:
The Spirit says, ‘I have sent them’. In the Scriptures God often sends messengers who are not what anyone expected. The Law also asked Israel to care for the outsider who came to them: “Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners” (Exodus 23:9).

The Law also asked for more than one witness to settle a matter: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Peter brings witnesses with him. He seems to sense that what is about to happen will need to be told and believed.
passages.asks: Peter did not yet understand the whole vision, but he obeyed the next step: open the door, give the guests a meal, go with them in the morning. Ask what the next small step of obedience is for you, even before you understand where it leads.

passages.happening:
The next day Peter arrives in Caesarea. Cornelius is waiting, with his relatives and close friends gathered (verse 24). As Peter comes in, Cornelius falls at his feet to worship him. But Peter lifts him up. “Stand up,” he says, “I am only a man myself” (verse 26).

Inside, many people are gathered. Peter says, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him. But God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean” (verse 28). So he has come without objection, and he asks why they sent for him.

Cornelius tells of the angel four days before, at the ninth hour, and ends, “Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to tell us” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Cornelius kneels to Peter, as people in that world might kneel to a great man or a god. Peter refuses it at once. No apostle accepts worship in Acts. When Paul and Barnabas are mistaken for gods in Lystra (14:14-15), they do the same.

Then Peter says something honest and hard: ‘You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him.’ The Law of Moses nowhere forbids a Jew to enter a Gentile's house. But many devout Jews avoided eating in Gentile homes, where food would not be prepared by the food laws and might have been offered to idols. How strictly this was kept varied from place to place and person to person. It was a real wall.

Peter has now understood his vision. It was not mainly about animals. It was about people: ‘I should not call any man impure or unclean.’

Cornelius's answer is one of the best descriptions of a listening heart in the Bible. ‘We are all here in the presence of God to listen.’ He has gathered his family and friends, not to see a show, but to hear.
passages.ot:
Peter's words, ‘I am only a man myself’, echo a long theme of Scripture: worship belongs to God alone. “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3).

The wall Peter steps over had a purpose in the Law, to keep Israel holy. But God had always meant Israel's calling to bless the nations. He told Abraham, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The book of Jonah ends with God asking his angry prophet, “should I not care about the great city of Nineveh” (Jonah 4:11)? Jonah once went down to Joppa to run away from God's call to that foreign city (Jonah 1:3). Now Peter, whom Jesus called ‘Simon son of Jonah’ (Matthew 16:17), leaves Joppa and goes to the foreigners willingly.
passages.asks: Peter walked through a door he had avoided all his life, because God told him to. Ask which doors you have never walked through, and why. And take Cornelius's words as a pattern for how to come to Scripture or to church: ‘we are all here in the presence of God to listen’.

passages.happening:
Peter begins: “I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism, but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right” (verses 34-35).

He tells the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, “who is Lord of all” (verse 36). He tells how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how Jesus “went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with Him” (verse 38).

“We are witnesses of all that He did,” Peter says (verse 39). They put Jesus to death “by hanging Him on a tree”, but God raised him on the third day and caused him to be seen by chosen witnesses, “by us who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead” (verse 41). Jesus commanded them to preach that he is the one appointed by God “to judge the living and the dead” (verse 42). “All the prophets testify about Him that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name” (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
‘Favoritism’ translates a Greek word that means, word for word, ‘receiving a face’: judging people by who they are or how they look. Peter says God does not do that. He has learned it this week, on a roof and at a gate.

The sermon is a short telling of the whole story of Jesus, from John's baptism to the resurrection and the coming judgment. Peter assumes his hearers already know the outline: ‘You yourselves know what has happened throughout Judea’ (verse 37). Caesarea was close enough to have heard the news.

Notice ‘Lord of all’. In a city named after Caesar, Peter calls Jesus Lord of all: Jew and Gentile, ruler and soldier.

‘They put Him to death’: Peter means those in Jerusalem who handed Jesus over, with the Romans who carried out the crucifixion. As in his earlier sermons, a Jew is speaking of what was done in his own city, and offering forgiveness to everyone who believes. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how such verses were later misused against Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

‘Welcomes those from every nation who fear Him’ does not mean that good people do not need Jesus. The angel sent Cornelius to Peter so that he could hear ‘a message by which you and all your household will be saved’ (11:14). Christians differ on what this means for people who never hear of Jesus. The Honest Answer ‘What about those who never heard?’ sets out the views.
passages.ot:
Peter's first sentence comes from the Law. Moses said the LORD is “the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17). What Peter knew about God's justice, he now sees in God's welcome.

‘God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit’ echoes Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor” (Isaiah 61:1), the passage Jesus read in Nazareth (Luke 4:18).

‘Hanging Him on a tree’ points to the Law: “anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse” (Deuteronomy 21:23). Paul would later say that Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

And ‘all the prophets testify about Him’ sums up the whole Old Testament as a witness to Jesus.
passages.asks: ‘God does not show favoritism.’ Ask whom you treat with favoritism, and whom you overlook. Church, family and friendship all have their ways of ‘receiving a face’. The God who welcomed a Roman soldier into his family asks his people to welcome the same way.

passages.happening:
“While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard his message” (verse 44). The Jewish believers who had come with Peter are astonished that the gift of the Spirit has been poured out “even on the Gentiles” (verse 45). They hear them speaking in tongues and praising God (verse 46).

Peter says, “Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!” (verse 47). So he orders that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they ask him to stay for a few days (verse 48).
passages.hearers:
Peter is interrupted. He has not even finished his sermon. God does not wait for him.

The ‘circumcised believers’ are the Jewish believers from Joppa. They are not hostile; they are amazed. They had assumed that the Spirit was for Israel, and for Gentiles only once they became part of Israel. Now they hear these Gentiles speaking in tongues and praising God, just as the believers did at Pentecost (2:4).

Peter's question settles it. If God has given them the Spirit, who can refuse them the water? Baptism follows, in the name of Jesus Christ, without circumcision.

Then the last line: ‘they asked him to stay for a few days’. Staying means eating together, sleeping under one roof. Peter, who had ‘never eaten anything impure’, now sits at a Gentile table. The vision has come true in a household.
passages.ot:
Joel had promised that God would pour out his Spirit “on all people” (Joel 2:28), and Peter had quoted it at Pentecost (2:17). Now the ‘all’ reaches the Gentiles.

The prophets had long pictured the nations turning to Israel's God: “All the families of the nations will bow down before Him” (Psalm 22:27). Isaiah's servant was to be “a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6). In a soldier's house in Caesarea, that light comes in.
passages.hard:
In Acts 2, Peter said, ‘Repent and be baptized’, and promised the Spirit (2:38). In Samaria, the Spirit came after baptism, when the apostles laid hands on the believers (8:14-17). Here, the Spirit comes before baptism, while Peter is still speaking. Later, in Ephesus, he comes after baptism and the laying on of hands (19:5-6). Which is the pattern?

This is exactly why the book page's part ‘What Acts is not’ warns against making one scene the rule for all. Acts shows the Spirit coming in different orders as the good news crosses new lines: to Jews, to Samaritans, to Gentiles. Churches read this in the ways set out in the notes on 2:38 and 8:14-17. Some see a normal pattern in one scene and special moments in others. Others see the variety itself as the lesson: God is free, and he will not be boxed in by the church's order.

What is plain in this scene is why God acted as he did. Peter later explains it at the council in Jerusalem: “God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us” (15:8). No one could now say that these Gentiles were second-class believers.
passages.asks: God poured out his Spirit on people the church was not yet sure about. Ask whether you have ever decided someone could not belong, and God proved you wrong. And notice what Peter did when he saw it. He did not argue. He baptized them and stayed for dinner.
